newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish inflation to tick higher into 1998-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Irish inflation to tick higher into 1998-analysts.

text.p: Ireland has enjoyed an enviable combination of high growth and low inflation in recent years but while most analysts are confident that growth should remain strong, they are less optimistic about inflation.

Most expect consumer price inflation to tick up from its current level of 1.2 percent over the balance of the year, mainly due to the effects of recent Irish pound weakness against sterling and a fall in the trade-weighted index.
But analysts are divided on how high the inflation rate could go with forecasts for average inflation next year ranging from 2.5 percent to 4.4 percent.

In an economic review published on Wednesday, the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) said it expects inflation to average 1.75 percent by the end of the year, increasing further to 2.5 percent next year, at the lower end of expectations

Current fears concerning the inflationary effects of the sterling exchange rate are probably exaggerated, the ESRI said, noting that the trade-weighted value of the Irish pound has at least as great an influence on Irish prices.
It also notes that the inflation rate, in a small open economy like Ireland's, is largely externally determined and the international environment remains one of low inflation.

But others fear the ESRI's estimates may be too low and overly dependent on a reversal of current exchange rate trends which have seen the Irish pound lose 16 percent against sterling in the last year.
Riada Stockbrokers expects inflation to average 1.7 percent this year, rising to 3.0 percent next year.
"I would certainly expect inflation to tick up because of what's happened on foreign exchange markets," economist Padhraic Garvey told Reuters.
"The exchange rate effect takes between six and nine months to feed through and it should start to really feed through in the first and second quarter of next year."
Davy Stockbrokers' forecasts are even higher with the broker expecting inflation to peak at five percent in mid-1998 before edging down to average 4.4 percent overall next year.

"Reflecting the effects of the Irish pound's 16 percent depreciation against sterling over the past twelve months and assuming no more than a modest reversal of this decline throughout the forecast period, we expect CPI inflation to accelerate sharply over the balance of 1997 and through the first part of next year," Davy said in an economic review published on Tuesday.
But NCB Stockbrokers notes that the punt had been falling against sterling since last October and the price effect has not yet shown up.
"We are not persuaded that there is this particular relationship with sterling at all," NCB economist Dermot O'Brien said.

"What people have been missing is the inflation adjustment in the UK to sterling...Either sterling prices are adjusting to the world level because they are price-takers on the world market or we have the opportunity to source elsewhere."
NCB expects an average inflation rate of 1.5 percent this year but the key factor in determining the outlook heading into next year is whether or not the punt is revalued, O'Brien says.

If the rate chosen for entry to the single currency is the punt's ERM central parity of 2.41 marks, nearly 10 percent below current trading levels, and the Irish pound falls back toward this level, the punt's trade-weighted index would drop sharply.
This could then push inflation into the three to four percent range next year, NCB said.
"The whole thing crucially depends on whether the punt is revalued. If we revalue, inflation will stay below two percent next year," O'Brien said.
